issues.legal_issue: The procedure for executing an order for sale of mortgaged property made in a special financial-corporation proceeding includes the mortgagor’s right to seek redemption under the ordinary civil execution rules where applying that procedure is practicable and the right of redemption remains unextinguished.
material_facts: The mortgagor had mortgaged property as security for a loan from a financial corporation, and the corporation sought attachment and sale of the property after default through a special statutory process.
The property was sold at auction under an order made in that process, and a later auction was also held while proceedings concerning the first sale remained pending.
The corporation accepted payment in full satisfaction of its claim, and the mortgagor deposited the amounts required for the purchasers under the redemption procedure.
No party showed why applying the ordinary execution rules governing redemption would be impracticable, and the mortgagor’s right of redemption had not been extinguished.
issues.conclusion: The redemption procedure in Order 34 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure applied to execution of the sale order. The mortgagor’s application was allowed, the challenged sale orders were set aside, and consequential repayment and satisfaction directions were made.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(8) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 makes the Code’s procedure for attachment or sale in execution applicable as far as practicable, treating the corporation as decree-holder and the debtor as judgment-debtor for that execution purpose. This legal fiction is limited to its purpose and cannot be extended beyond execution. Order 34 Rule 5, read with Order 21, therefore applies to execution of the sale order unless its application is shown to be impracticable. Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act preserves redemption unless extinguished by act of the parties or decree of a court. The Court relied on Gujarat State Financial Corporation v. Natson Manufacturing Co. (P) Ltd., M/s Everest Industrial Corporation v. Gujarat State Financial Corporation, Mhadagonda Ramgonda Patil v. Shripal Balwant Rainade, and the legal-fiction principles in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council, The Bengal Immunity Company Ltd. v. State of Bihar, Commissioner of Income-tax v. Amarchand N. Shroff, and Commissioner of Income Tax v. Vedilal Lallubhai.

rule.if: corporation_security_sale_proceeding and sale_order_executed_through_ordinary_execution_procedure and redemption_right_unextinguished and redemption_procedure_practicable

predicates.corporation_security_sale_proceeding: A creditor corporation pursued attachment and sale of property given as loan security through a special statutory proceeding.
predicates.sale_order_executed_through_ordinary_exe: The sale order was carried out using the ordinary civil procedure for execution of a decree, so far as practicable.
predicates.redemption_right_unextinguished: The mortgagor’s right to redeem had not been extinguished by an act of the parties or a court decree.
predicates.redemption_procedure_practicable: No circumstance was shown that made the ordinary execution procedure for redemption impracticable to apply.

issues.definition: When a corporation pursues a special statutory sale of loan-security property, the sale order is executed through ordinary execution procedure, the redemption right remains, and the redemption procedure is practicable, the mortgagor may seek redemption during execution.

issues.legal_issue: Confirmation of an execution sale does not prevent a mortgagor from seeking redemption while an appeal challenging the sale remains pending and the right of redemption has not been extinguished.
material_facts: The mortgagor challenged the first auction sale, and the challenge was initially allowed before being reversed on appeal.
The High Court confirmed the first sale while an appeal against its order was pending before the Supreme Court.
A subsequent sale had been held subject to a direction that it not be confirmed.
The mortgagor sought redemption while the appeals remained pending, and the right of redemption had not been extinguished.
issues.conclusion: The confirmation of the first sale had not become absolute while the appeal remained pending, and the mortgagor could still invoke the redemption procedure. The later sale, which had not been confirmed, could not stand once the redemption relief was granted.
issues.legal_principle: Order 34 Rule 5 permits payment before confirmation of sale. An order confirming a sale after dismissal of a challenge to the sale does not attain finality for this purpose while an appeal against that dismissal is pending. The Court relied on Chandra Mani v. Anarjan Bibi, Sri Ranga Nilayam Ramkrishan Rao v. Kandokari Chellayamma, S.V. Ramalingam v. K.E. Rajagopalan, and M. Sevugan Chettiar v. V.A. Narayana Raja. Under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, redemption is extinguished only in the circumstances specified there; Raghunath Singh v. Pt. Hansraj Kunwar and Mhadagonda Ramgonda Patil v. Shripal Balwant Rainade were also relied on concerning the survival and extinguishment of that right.

predicates.mortgage_execution_sale_proceeding: A sale of mortgaged property was being conducted in execution proceedings.
predicates.sale_challenge_appeal_pending: An appeal challenging the decision on an application to set aside the sale remained pending.
predicates.redemption_right_unextinguished: The mortgagor’s right to redeem had not been extinguished by an act of the parties or a court decree.

issues.definition: In an execution sale of mortgaged property, when an appeal challenging the sale remains pending and the redemption right survives, the mortgagor may seek redemption before the sale is final.

issues.legal_issue: A proceeding seeking attachment and sale of secured property under a special financial-corporation process is not a mortgage suit, and the order made in that proceeding is not a decree in such a suit.
material_facts: The financial corporation applied for relief following default on a loan secured by mortgaged property.
The relief sought was attachment and sale of the secured property, not a money decree, a preliminary decree for accounts, or enforcement of personal liability under the mortgage.
The statutory process provided for an order directing sale after attachment and a limited inquiry by the court.
issues.conclusion: The application was not equivalent to a suit for enforcement of a mortgage, and the resulting sale order was not an order in a mortgage suit; the proceeding was akin to an application for attachment of property at a stage after a decree.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 31 and 32 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 provide a special procedure for obtaining an order for attachment and sale and dispense with ordinary suit procedure up to that stage. The Court relied on Gujarat State Financial Corporation v. Natson Manufacturing Co. (P) Ltd., which characterized the proceeding as akin to an application for attachment in execution after a decree, and M/s Everest Industrial Corporation v. Gujarat State Financial Corporation.

predicates.special_corporation_recovery_proceeding: A creditor corporation used a special statutory proceeding to seek recovery following default on a secured loan.
predicates.relief_limited_to_security_sale: The relief sought was attachment and sale of secured property, rather than a money decree or enforcement of personal liability under the mortgage.

issues.definition: When a corporation uses a special recovery proceeding and seeks only attachment and sale of secured property, the proceeding is not a mortgage suit.
